newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia "lost" wallet test shows Singapore top.
newsitem.headline: Asia "lost" wallet test shows Singapore top.

text.p: Nine out of ten Singapore citizens returned dropped wallets stuffed with cash, but in Hong Kong only three out of ten wallets were recovered in an honesty test carried out in Asian cities by Readers Digest.
Larger cities fared worse on the honesty index, while people in smaller places returned planted wallets with regularity all over Asia, results from the experiment showed.
"I know how hard it is to earn money, I wouldn't feel right taking somebody else's money," explained an illiterate fisherman from the South Indian town of Trivandrum.

Readers Digest surreptitiously scattered 140 wallets all over Asia, each containing a name, local address and phone number, family pictures, notes, coupons and cash ranging from the local equivalent of US$10 to US$50.
The magazine staff then watched to see what happened.
South Koreans in Seoul returned six out of the 10 dropped wallets, while those in Inchon returned eight.
"All I could think about was that we must return the wallet to the owner as quickly as possible," said schoolgirl Jang Yeo Jin.
Bombay, Bangkok, Taipei and Kajang in Malaysia scored 50 percent on the honesty charts, with most people saying they would not keep what was not rightfully theirs.

Honesty had little relation to wealth or status, the survey found, and hidden staff watched several well-heeled people in a number of cities walk away with wallets without making any attempt to contact the rightful owner.
A large number of those who returned wallets cited religious beliefs. "Being a Muslim, I'm aware of temptation and how to overcome it," said a fruit stall owner in Malaysia.
About 57 percent of the wallets were returned, compared with 58 percent in Europe in a similar experiment and 67 percent in the United States.
